title: Love as strong as death (Song of Songs 8:6–7)
hook: many waters cannot quench love; a book of love poetry in the Bible

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher's last poem, the silver cord and the golden bowl. Your line: remember, while you're young.

Some people open the Bible expecting rules and are startled to find this. A woman searching the city streets at night for the one she loves. A man comparing her hair to a flock of goats coming down a mountainside, which was a compliment. Gardens, spices, vineyards, doves, a knock at the door. Two voices, longing for each other, out loud. A whole book of love poetry, right after Ecclesiastes. And near its end, the woman says something so strong it's still read at weddings.
screen: `SEARCHING THE CITY AT NIGHT.` → `HAIR LIKE A FLOCK OF GOATS.` → `A WHOLE BOOK OF LOVE POETRY.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death." A seal in the ancient world was a stamp carved in stone, worn on a cord around the neck or on a ring. It was your signature, your identity. Set me as a seal on your heart means: carry me, let me be the mark you press into everything. And love is as strong as death. Not stronger. As strong. Death is the one thing nothing escapes, and love, she says, holds on just as hard. Then: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." In the Bible, the great waters are chaos, the flood, the sea that swallows. Love isn't put out by them. And if a man offered everything he owned for love, he'd be laughed at. Love can't be bought. Now a surprise: God is barely named in this book, if at all. Some read one word in verse six, describing love's flame, as containing a short form of God's name; many others read it simply as a mighty flame. So why is it in the Bible? Readers answer more than one way. Jewish tradition has long read it as the love between God and Israel; a famous rabbi called it the holy of holies among the writings. Christian readers from the early church on have read it as the love between Christ and the church, or God and the soul. And readers also honor it as human love, desire and faithfulness, celebrated as good.
screen: `SET ME AS A SEAL UPON THINE HEART.` · `AS STRONG AS DEATH, NOT STRONGER.` · `MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE.` · `GOD, ISRAEL, CHRIST, OR TWO PEOPLE?` · then, large: `LOVE IS STRONG AS DEATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, a partner, a parent, a child, a friend of many years, and think of the floods it has come through: a move, an argument, an illness, a loss. Notice that it's still here, and picture them carrying you like a seal on the heart, and you carrying them. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Seal. The stamp a person wore as their signature in the ancient world, the image the Song of Songs uses for love strong as death, carried on the heart.
Your line: many waters cannot quench love. Neither can the floods drown it. That's day four hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Song of Songs 8:6–7 is a frequent reading at Christian weddings; the book has a long history of devotional reading as a picture of God's love, and in Jewish practice it is read at Passover.

notes: Editor pass (y2 review): the human-love reading was introduced as 'what it plainly is', which ranked it above the Jewish and Christian readings; now all three stand side by side. Cut 'eight chapters long', 'wedding invitations and gravestones', and the practice line telling the listener what they feel. Review updated to match day 457's revised carry.
Rabbi Akiva's saying (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5) that 'all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies' is paraphrased and the rabbi is not named in the voice. Confirm.
Shalhevetyah (8:6): KJV 'a most vehement flame'; some read the -yah ending as the divine name ('flame of the LORD'), others as an intensifier. Presented as divided. Confirm.
Song of Songs read at Passover (Ashkenazi custom, Shabbat of Pesach). Confirm.
Christian allegorical reading (Origen, Bernard of Clairvaux) is summarized without names. Confirm fair to Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant readers.
Original-language line: עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה (8:6). Confirm the pointing and transliteration.
